question: When visiting the islands of Pico and Faial in the Azores, I met a number of farmers whose farms are being adversely affected by the proliferation of birds such as the collared dove, the wood pigeon and the blackbird: protected species that have multiplied to such an extent as to be considered pests. The farmers told me that, in recent years, these birds have inflicted thousands of euros’ worth of damage to the wine and horticulture sectors and to maize crops. In light of the above: 1.
What steps can be taken to prevent these species from attacking farms in future?
What support can be granted to the farmers who have suffered huge losses as a result of these attacks?
answer: 1. The Commission is aware of the adverse impacts on vineyards and the horticulture sector in some regions caused by increasing populations of some bird species. Wild birds are protected under Article 5 of the Birds Directive (1), since they are part of the EU natural heritage.
Member States may grant derogations from that provision under Article 9 (1) (a), where there is no other satisfactory solution, such as scaring techniques, to prevent serious damage to crops. 2.

Support may be provided through the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) for preventive actions and investments aimed at mitigating the risk of damages to the farming activity caused by protected animals, improving the conditions for their coexistence.

Moreover, further specific actions aimed at promoting the coexistence of wild animals — including birds — and the farming activity could be supported, to different extent, under other EAFRD funded interventions (e.g. knowledge transfer, training, advisory services, risk management and cooperation between rural actors).

However, such support must be programmed by the Member States under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) instruments approved by the Commission in order to be paid. Furthermore, EU State aid rules (2) allow Member States to compensate up to 100% of direct and indirect costs of damages caused by protected animals. It is also possible to finance up to 100% of preventive measures under these rules.
There is equally aid for the payment of insurance premiums. For concrete information, the Honourable Member is invited to contact the Portuguese Authorities (3).

Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds (OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7).
